title: Street food and markets in Mauritius
summary: Where the markets are and when they are open, as the councils that run them state: Port Louis, Flacq, Quatre Bornes, Curepipe, Rose Hill, Beau Bassin, Vacoas, Goodlands and Mahebourg. What is sold, where the food courts are, and the hygiene rules that bind anyone who sells food. Checked on 20 November 2026.
audience: Visitors and residents planning a trip to a market, and anyone who wants to know what rules a food seller has to follow.

sections.heading: Where do you find street food in Mauritius?

blocks.text: You find it at street stalls, in the food kiosks and food courts of the public markets, and at fairs. The Mauritius Tourism Promotion Authority says the island has an incredible street food scene and calls Port Louis one of the best cities in the world for street food. It points visitors to the Port Louis Central Market, where kiosks sell samosas, dholl puri, sweet pastries and alouda.

Public markets and fairs are run by the municipal and district councils, which enforce their own market regulations and post health inspectors. The fixed markets are open every day. The fairs are held on set days of the week. The days and hours below are the ones a council states on its own website. Where a council states none, we say so.

sections.heading: When is the Port Louis Central Market open?

blocks.text: The City Council of Port Louis gives these hours for the Central Market: Monday to Saturday from 5 am to 6 pm in summer and from 5.30 am to 6 pm in winter. On Sundays and public holidays it opens at the same time and closes at noon. The Jinnah Market keeps the same hours.

The tourism authority also calls it the Bazaar Port Louis and says this is where the locals shop. Stalls are piled with tropical fruit and vegetables, the street food kiosks are inside, stalls just outside sell clothes and bags, and the first floor sells locally made crafts. The market is a short walk from the Caudan Waterfront and next to Chinatown.

items: Abercrombie Market and Fair, at Sainte Croix: Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, 5.30 am to 6 pm.
Ibrahim Abdoollah Market and Fair: Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, 6 am to 6 pm.
Pointe aux Sables Market and Fair: Sundays only, 5.30 am to noon.
Monneron Fair: Monday to Sunday. The council gives no hours.

blocks.text: The tourism authority calls Central Flacq the largest outdoor market in Mauritius and says Wednesdays and Sundays are the best days to go, because all the stalls are open. The Municipal Council of Vacoas-Phoenix says its fair in the town centre is one of the biggest in the country, with more than 1,300 stalls and spaces, but gives no days on the page. The District Council of Grand Port runs three markets and fairs, at Mahebourg, Plaine Magnien and Rose Belle, and the District Council of Savanne runs five markets and five fairs. Neither states the days.

The same council page for Beau Bassin and Rose Hill lists six markets and fairs: Rose Hill, Beau Bassin, Da Patten, Plaisance, Chebel and New Arab Town. Da Patten and Chebel open at 7 am, the others at 6 am.

sections.heading: What is sold, and where are the food courts?

blocks.text: The fixed markets sell fresh food by section. Flacq lists poultry, fish, goat, pork, beef, venison, vegetables, fruit and general retail, with a separate craft market. Rose Hill keeps fish, meat, pork and poultry in one section and vegetables, bread, cakes and flowers in another. Vacoas has stalls for goat and mutton, beef, fish and poultry, and an auction space where vegetables from all over the country are sold to traders. The fairs add haberdashery and general retail.

items: Quatre Bornes: a food court open every day from 6 am to 6 pm.
Flacq: a food court in the fixed market, and another at the Lallmatie Fair.
Vacoas: a food court with three booths and a dining hall.
Plaisance Fair, Rose Hill: a kiosk in the yard for cakes and non-alcoholic drinks.
Port Louis: the street food kiosks of the Central Market.

sections.heading: What hygiene rules bind people who sell food?

blocks.text: The same law covers a market stall, a food cart and a hotel kitchen. The Food Act 2022 defines food premises widely enough to include a street, an open space, a bicycle, a tricycle and any vehicle used to prepare or sell food. The Food Regulations 2024, in force since 9 September 2024, set the daily rules. They are enforced by authorised officers of the Ministry of Health and Wellness, who may enter premises, take samples, and seize or destroy food.

items: Everyone who sells, prepares, cooks, serves or delivers food for sale must hold a valid Food Handler's Certificate at all times.
Food ready to eat must be packed, wrapped or covered against flies, dust and contamination. Wrapping paper may carry no printing or writing apart from the label.
A seller may not blow into a paper bag or wet a finger with saliva to open one.
Ready to eat food is picked up with tongs or another device, unless the nature of the food makes that impracticable.
A street food vendor's stall, table, bicycle, tricycle or cart must be designed or adapted for the food sold. The food travels in a clean receptacle that stays covered except while it is being sold.

A food vehicle needs a sink with potable water, a wash-hand basin with soap, refrigeration for perishable food, a covered bin and a waste water tank. Ready to eat food is sold in disposable containers.

Perishable food, such as cooked rice, meat, seafood, dairy and cut fruit, is kept at 4 °C or below, or at 60 °C or above, or at another temperature at which, according to the operator, the food is not adversely affected.
Food handlers keep hands, hair, nails and clothing clean, wear a clean overall and a hair covering, and wear no rings, watch or nail varnish. They may not eat, smoke or spit while handling food.
No food may be prepared or sold near public toilets or in an insanitary place, and single-use containers and drinking straws may not be reused.

blocks.text: An officer can serve an improvement notice, or a prohibition order where food is a hazard to health. The seller has 7 days to appeal against an order. A person who commits an offence under the Act or the regulations faces a fine of up to Rs 100,000 and up to 2 years in prison. Smoking is also banned in markets, and by anyone preparing, serving or selling food in premises open to the public.

sections.heading: Who may sell food on the street or in a market?

blocks.text: The Food Act says no person may operate a food business without being registered under the Business Registration Act. The business registry lists the sale of foodstuffs along the road, from a mobile unit or in markets and fairs among the activities that need approval from the Ministry of Local Government, and sale on the beach among those that need approval from the Ministry of Tourism. Under the Local Government Act a hawker may not trade without an authorisation from the council.

Market stalls are not sold freely. Beau Bassin-Rose Hill and Vacoas-Phoenix both say vacant stalls are advertised in the press, and that an applicant must live in the town, be unemployed and work on the stall in person.

sections.heading: Can you bargain, and what should you check?

blocks.text: The tourism authority says you are welcome to bargain with a stallholder in a marketplace, and should always confirm the price before you buy. On the beach it advises against buying from unauthorised persons: if in doubt, ask to see the operating licence. If a stall worries you, the council's market office is the first place to complain. Curepipe gives 676 2407 and Beau Bassin-Rose Hill gives 413 7600 for information and complaints.
